title: Alzheimer's drug access varies by race, vulnerability, and health status
content: The first disease-modifying drugs for Alzheimer's disease are designed to slow cognitive decline by targeting amyloid plaques in the brain. However, a new study indicates that patients do not have equal opportunities to receive these treatments. According to the research, race, vulnerability, and health status are key factors that shape access to the medication.
summary: New Alzheimer's drugs slow cognitive decline by targeting amyloid plaques in the brain. A new study indicates that race, vulnerability, and health status shape patient access to these treatments.

title: Harvard team develops faster antibody screening for cancer treatments
content: A research team led by scientists at Harvard Medical School, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute has developed a new antibody screening method. This approach is designed to accelerate the process of identifying and engineering cancer-fighting therapies.
summary: Researchers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute have developed a faster method to identify cancer-fighting therapies. The antibody screening approach aims to accelerate the engineering of immune-based treatments.

title: Study finds prebiotic fiber helps girls build more bone
content:
A one-year clinical trial led by Florida International University nutrition researcher Cristina Palacios found that prebiotic fiber supplements can enhance bone development in girls. The study compared participants who added the supplement to their regular diets against a control group that received a placebo.

The results indicated that girls taking the prebiotic fiber supplement built more bone over the course of the year than those who took the placebo.
summary: A clinical trial led by Cristina Palacios at Florida International University found that girls who took a prebiotic fiber supplement for a year built more bone. The results showed these girls built more bone than girls who took a placebo.

title: Protein modification reverses cancer muscle wasting in preclinical study
content:
Cachexia, a severe form of muscle wasting affecting up to 80% of cancer patients, is driven by pro-inflammatory cytokines released by tumor cells. Known as cancer-induced cachexia (CIC), this condition is responsible for 30% to 50% of all cancer-related deaths worldwide, earning it the nickname "final disease" due to the absence of curative treatments.

A preclinical study indicates that protein modification can partially reverse this cancer-related muscle wasting, offering a potential avenue for addressing a condition currently without a cure.
summary: A preclinical study found that protein modification partially reverses cancer-related muscle wasting, known as cachexia. This condition affects up to 80% of cancer patients and is caused by pro-inflammatory signaling molecules released by tumor cells.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study links nature contact to positive food relationship
content: A study led by Anglia Ruskin University (ARU) suggests that contact with natural environments may help individuals develop healthier eating habits. Published in the journal Body Image, the research provides the first evidence that exposure to nature can influence people's relationship with food.
summary: A study led by Anglia Ruskin University found that contact with natural environments may help people develop healthier eating habits. Published in the journal Body Image, this is the first research to provide evidence that exposure to nature can influence people's relationship with food.

content:

content: A new report from People with Disability Australia (PWDA), the national disability rights and advocacy organization, states that employers must take greater action to remove barriers preventing women with disability from advancing into leadership roles. summary: A new report from People with Disability Australia states that employers must remove barriers preventing women with disability from reaching leadership roles. Researchers in the report identify six lessons to help drive change in this area.

title: North Sea Heat Wave Triggers Underwater Plankton Bloom Missed by Satellites
content:
Satellites are frequently used by scientists to monitor ocean responses to marine heat waves by detecting changes in ocean color, which indicate shifts in phytoplankton populations. These microscopic organisms are essential to marine food webs and the global carbon cycle, yet satellite observations are limited to the ocean's surface.

In the North Sea, a recent heat wave triggered an underwater plankton bloom that was largely missed by these satellite systems due to their inability to detect activity below the surface.
summary: Scientists use satellites to detect changes in ocean color during marine heat waves. Satellites can only see the ocean's surface, missing underwater plankton blooms in the North Sea.

title: Battle of Neville's Cross: 1346 Capture of King David II Outside Durham
content:
On October 17, 1346, the Battle of Neville’s Cross took place outside Durham in northeast England. This conflict served as a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history, resulting in the capture of King David II of Scotland.

Despite its significant impact on relations between England, Scotland, and France, the battle remains little-known to many people.
summary: The Battle of Neville's Cross was fought on Oct. 17, 1346 outside Durham in northeast England. The battle captured King David II of Scotland, marking a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history.

title: AI converts scrap impurities into ingredients for stronger recycled iron
content:
AI technology is being applied to transform impurities found in scrap metal into useful ingredients that can produce stronger recycled iron.  

Global metal output reaches roughly 2 billion metric tons each year, a level that underpins industry, infrastructure and the energy sector. That scale of production accounts for an estimated 40 % of industrial greenhouse‑gas emissions and about 10 % of worldwide energy consumption.  

Expanding the use of recycled metals therefore offers a pathway to lessen the environmental footprint of metal manufacturing and to reduce dependence on imports of scarce, strategically important raw materials.
summary: AI can transform impurities in scrap metal into useful components for producing stronger recycled iron. Using more recycled metals could lower the 40% of industrial greenhouse gas emissions and 10% of global energy consumption tied to primary metal production.

title: New paper traces CDK research evolution and next-gen cancer therapies
content: A new paper traces the evolution of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK) research, marking more than 30 years since the direct connection between the molecular machinery controlling cell division and cancer was established. The study outlines the next generation of CDK-targeted therapies, extending from the initial discovery of CDK9 to applications in precision medicine and beyond.
summary: A new paper outlines the next generation of CDK-targeted therapies for cancer. The publication also traces the evolution of cyclin-dependent kinase research over more than 30 years.

title: Single 2D crystal becomes transistor with built-in insulation and contacts
content:
A new development in semiconductor technology involves a single two-dimensional crystal that transforms into a transistor with built-in insulation and electrical contacts. Traditional transistors require several fundamentally different materials, including a semiconductor to carry current, an insulating dielectric to control it, and metallic contacts for current entry and exit.

Integrating these distinct components becomes increasingly difficult as semiconductor devices approach the atomic scale. The new single-crystal approach addresses this challenge by combining the necessary functional elements within one material structure.
summary: A transistor typically requires multiple different materials, including a semiconductor, insulating dielectric, and metallic contacts. Integrating these components is difficult as semiconductor devices approach the atomic scale.

title: Building trust in governments through digital platforms
content:
Global surveys indicate that a significant portion of the population reports a lack of trust in their respective governments. This decline in confidence has been particularly notable in recent decades across Latin America, North America, and Africa.

As these regions experience falling trust levels, the focus has turned to methods for restoring public confidence. Digital platforms are being examined as a potential tool for governments to rebuild this trust with their citizens.
summary: Around the world, many people report distrusting their government. In some places, such as Latin America, North America and Africa, trust in government has declined in recent decades.

title: Satellite data offers clues on how glacial ice cliffs will collapse as climate warms
content: Scientists have not yet determined with certainty how the towering ice cliffs at the leading edges of glaciers will behave as global temperatures rise. However, recent analysis of satellite data provides initial clues regarding the stability of these glacial ice cliffs.
summary: The behavior of towering ice cliffs at the leading edge of glaciers remains uncertain as the climate warms. Satellite data provides some clues regarding how these cliffs may collapse.

title: New computational approach reveals how cells communicate to assemble tissues
content:

The findings could accelerate stem cell engineering and improve the development of disease models. Additionally, the research may inform the creation of new therapies by clarifying the mechanisms of cellular communication.
summary: A new computational approach reveals how cells communicate to assemble into tissues. This discovery could accelerate stem cell engineering, improve disease models, and inform therapies.

summary: MIT's Center for Transportation and Logistics reports that corporate sustainability commitments are at a record high. However, governance gaps and external disruptions prevent the execution of these commitments.

title: Neanderthal shoulder wound in Iraqi Kurdistan may be oldest spear kill evidence
content:
Archaeologists excavating the Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan have identified a Neanderthal adult who died more than 70,000 years ago with a smooth round hole in the shoulder blade. This distinctive injury, described as a “kill shot,” may constitute the oldest evidence to date of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear.

The skeletal remains of the adult and other Neanderthals were recovered from beneath nearly 8 meters of rock and sediment. The discovery provides significant insight into prehistoric hunting practices and the physical capabilities of early human ancestors.
summary: An adult Neanderthal excavated from Shanidar cave in Iraqi Kurdistan died more than 70,000 years ago with a distinctive shoulder injury. This wound may be the oldest evidence so far of a human ancestor being killed by a wooden spear.

title: NASA Satellites Track Historic 2026 El Niño Development
content: NASA is closely monitoring the development of the 2026 El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific. This phenomenon, which emerges roughly every two to seven years, is described as being rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system.
summary: NASA is closely monitoring a 2026 El Niño event described as rarer than a solar eclipse and more powerful than any single storm system. This natural climate pattern involves warmer-than-normal water temperatures in parts of the equatorial Pacific and typically emerges every two to seven years.

title: NASA to Support JAXA's MMX Mission to Study Mars' Moons
content:

The primary objectives of the MMX mission are to characterize the two moons and determine their origin. Additionally, the mission is designed to deliver a sample, contributing to the scientific understanding of these celestial bodies.
summary: NASA is playing an important role in JAXA's MMX mission to advance understanding of Mars' moons. The mission aims to characterize and determine the origin of Phobos and Deimos while delivering a sample.

title: Trump posts AI-edited photo of White House restoration work
content:

summary: President Donald Trump posted a series of photos on Truth Social showing White House renovations, but one image appears to be modified with AI. The photo was flagged by Google's AI detector as made or edited with OpenAI, and users noted discrepancies in the number of steps shown.

title: Amazon Devices Chief Panos Panay Envisions AI Devices Replacing Apps
content:
Amazon devices chief Panos Panay spoke at TechCrunch Disrupt about a future in which ambient AI devices operate in the background, anticipating users’ needs without requiring explicit commands.  

Panay said that these AI devices would replace the need to use apps by continuously monitoring context and responding proactively.
summary: At TechCrunch Disrupt, Amazon devices chief Panos Panay spoke about a future where ambient AI devices operate in the background. He said these devices would anticipate users' needs instead of waiting for commands.

title: Meta launches Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model for Macs
content:
Meta has announced the release of an open‑weight AI model designed to run on Mac computers. The new model, called Muse Spark Open, is set to operate locally on Apple silicon.

The launch is a joint effort between Meta and Apple. Meta’s social media platform is providing the model, while Apple will enable it to run natively on its silicon chips.

The announcement marks the first time Meta has offered an AI model that can be executed directly on Mac hardware.
summary: Meta and Apple have teamed up to launch Muse Spark Open, an open-weight AI model. The model runs locally on Apple silicon.

title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay stresses learning from failures
content:
Amazon devices chief Panos Panay said that learning from failure is a key part of building products.  

Panay explained that it is possible to recover and learn from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, when building products.  

His remarks underscore the importance of resilience in product development.
summary: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay said it is possible to recover and learn from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, when building products. He stressed the importance of failure and bouncing back from it.

title: Azerbaijan hosts rare summit of Middle East and Asian leaders on confidence-building
content:
Azerbaijan hosted a rare summit in Baku that brought together Middle East and Asian leaders, including those on opposing sides of conflicts. The gathering focused on “confidence‑building measures” aimed at easing tensions between the participants.

Attendees discussed how to address their differences while exploring opportunities for new transport corridors and economic realignments. The talks were framed against the backdrop of evolving global reshapes that could affect regional cooperation.

The summit underscored Azerbaijan’s role as a neutral venue for dialogue among diverse leaders.
summary: Middle East and Asian leaders, including those on opposing sides of conflicts, held a rare summit in Baku. The summit focused on confidence‑building measures, addressing differences and exploring opportunities for new transport corridors and economic realignments amid evolving global reshapes.
author: Euronews

title: Europeans more united on tougher China trade stance after German shift, says Noah Barkin
content:
Europeans are “far more united” on adopting a tougher stance toward China in trade matters, according to top expert Noah Barkin, who told Euronews that the shift came after Germany changed its position.

Barkin said the collective European position has strengthened following Germany’s move, signalling a more coordinated approach to China trade policy.
summary: Europeans are far more united on a tougher trade stance toward China after a shift by Germany. Top expert Noah Barkin said this in comments to Euronews.
author: Euronews

title: AI‑generated images of woman punched at Trump Ohio rally spread online
content:
A protester who heckled Donald Trump at his mid‑term rally in Youngstown, Ohio, was physically assaulted and removed from the event.  The incident has since been reproduced in fake AI‑generated photos that are circulating online.  

The images carry digital watermarks that identify them as AI‑generated.  Footage from the rally confirms that the woman was punched, but there is no evidence to support Trump’s claim that she was “paid” to disrupt his speech.  Trump also mocked the protester’s weight during the rally.  

Vedika Bahl explains the situation in Truth or Fake.
summary: A protester who heckled Donald Trump at his midterm rally in Youngstown, Ohio, was punched and removed from the event. Fake AI‑generated photos of the incident, marked with digital watermarks, are spreading online despite no evidence for Trump’s claim that the protester was paid to disrupt his speech.
author: France 24

title: Nobel laureate claims Donald Trump is openly financing Russia's war with Ukraine
content:
Nobel Peace laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk has accused former U.S. President Donald Trump of “openly financing Russia’s war with Ukraine.” In an interview with France 24’s Mark Owen, the director of the Centre for Civil Liberties said that the diesel‑supply deal with Moscow allows Trump to lift sanctions, thereby giving Russia “opportunities to earn more money.”  

Matviichuk added that the extra money would be converted into rockets and drones, leading to “additional deaths among the civilian population.”
summary: During an interview with France 24's Mark Owen, Nobel Peace laureate Oleksandra Matviichuk, Director of the Centre for Civil Liberties, said Donald Trump is openly financing Russia's war with Ukraine by lifting sanctions and enabling Russia to earn money through a diesel‑supply deal with Moscow. She added that the extra money would be converted into rockets and drones, causing additional civilian deaths.
author: France 24

title: Houthi missile and drone attack kills five at Yemen government palace in Aden
content:
A Houthi missile and drone strike on a palace in Yemen’s interim capital, Aden, killed at least five people and wounded 16 on Thursday, an official said.

The attack targeted the palace used by the internationally recognised Yemeni government. The strike resulted in the reported casualties, with no further details provided by the source.

The incident adds to the ongoing conflict in Yemen, according to the statement.
summary: At least five people were killed and 16 wounded in a Houthi missile and drone attack on the palace in Aden. The palace is used by Yemen's internationally recognized government, an official said.
author: France 24

title: Romanian MEP warns of European casualties after drones strike two tankers near Black Sea
content:
Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze and raising fresh security concerns along a vital shipping route used by Ukraine.

Speaking with FRANCE 24's Europe editor Armen Georgian, Romanian MEP Nicolae Stefanuta, co‑chair of the Group of the Greens, said the Danube delta region is facing a more intense threat from Russia than the Baltic States and that “it is clear that sooner or later we will have European casualties.”

The incident was reported on Thursday.
summary: Rescuers searched on Thursday for seven missing sailors after drones struck two chemical tankers near Romania's Black Sea coast, setting them ablaze. Romanian MEP Nicolae Stefanuta said the Danube delta region faces a more intense threat from Russia than the Baltic states and warned that European casualties are inevitable.
author: France 24

title: Kinshasa braces for potential conflict as Kabila joins M23
content:
Kinshasa is on alert after Joseph Kabila re‑emerged on the political scene by forming a new alliance with the M23 rebels, prompting Congolese leaders to choose sides as the city braces for possible conflict.

The United States called for restraint in Ethiopia, while a rights group warned that the fighting in Tigray is already taking a toll on civilians.

In cultural news, the season of art fairs has begun, highlighting the growing international visibility of African contemporary art.
summary: In tonight's edition, as Joseph Kabila returns to centre stage with a new alliance with the M23 rebels, political leaders in Congo are having to choose sides. Also, the US is calling for restraint in Ethiopia as a rights group warns that the conflict in Tigray is already taking a toll on civilians.

title: Saudi Arabia postpones major sporting events due to Houthi attacks
content:
Saudi Arabia has cancelled or postponed several major sporting events after repeated deadly attacks by Iran‑backed Houthi rebels on the kingdom’s airports and other infrastructure. The security concerns stemming from those attacks have disrupted the country’s event schedule.

FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen spoke with Guy Barton, a Visiting Fellow at Lancaster University and co‑creator and co‑host of The FootPol Podcast, about the impact of the Houthi strikes on Saudi sports planning.
summary: Several major sporting events in Saudi Arabia have been cancelled or postponed because repeated deadly attacks by Iran‑backed Houthi rebels have targeted the kingdom’s airports and infrastructure. FRANCE 24’s Mark Owen discusses the situation with Guy Barton, a Visiting Fellow at Lancaster University and co‑creator and co‑host of The FootPol Podcast.

title: EU member states brace for fierce seven-year budget negotiations
content:
European lawmakers have begun what is expected to be a long and intense negotiation over the European Union’s seven‑year budget. The talks are already fraught with disagreement among member states on how to allocate spending.

Divisions over spending priorities are compounded by pending elections in several countries, including France and Italy, which are adding pressure to the discussions in Brussels. The timing of these elections is influencing the urgency and direction of the budget talks.

In unrelated market news, AI stocks lost a trillion dollars in this week’s tech‑stock sell‑off. Ledger’s chief technology officer, Charles Guillemet, explained that advances in artificial intelligence are reshaping the security landscape.
summary: European lawmakers have started a long and fierce negotiation over the bloc's seven-year budget. Member states are divided on spending priorities, and pending elections in France and Italy are adding pressure to the talks in Brussels.
author: France 24

title: Oxfam sues French state over tax inequality, says billionaire pays less than nurse
content:
Oxfam has filed a lawsuit against the French state, alleging that the country’s tax system creates inequality and hampers funding for public services.  

At a press event, François Picard welcomed Layla Abdelké Yakoub, Tax Justice and Inequality Advocacy Officer at Oxfam France. Yakoub said a billionaire in France now pays proportionally less tax than a nurse or a firefighter, and she argued that the growing concentration of wealth and preferential tax treatment of the ultra‑rich undermine the constitutional principle of equality before taxation.  

Oxfam’s legal action challenges the foundations of France’s fiscal system, with Yakoub describing a widening gap between the government’s push to attract investment and its capacity to finance public services, combat poverty and support an ecological transition. The lawsuit targets the French state’s tax policies.
summary: Oxfam France has filed a lawsuit against the French state alleging that a billionaire pays proportionally less tax than a nurse or firefighter. Tax Justice and Inequality Advocacy Officer Layla Abdelké Yakoub says the fiscal system’s preferential treatment of the ultra‑rich undermines constitutional equality and hampers funding for public services, poverty relief and ecological transition.
author: France 24

title: Ethiopian forces expand control in Tigray, Eritrea denies troop movement
content:
Ethiopian forces have expanded their control in the Tigray region, according to recent reports. A militia operating in the area claimed that Eritrean forces suffered losses during the fighting.

Eritrea denied that any of its troops have moved inside northern Ethiopia, rejecting the militia’s assertion of Eritrean casualties. The United States called for de‑escalation of the conflict.

content:

content:

content: A recent poll indicates that right‑wing candidate Jair Bolsonaro holds a two‑percentage‑point lead over Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as Brazil approaches the presidential run‑off. The survey places Bolsonaro ahead of Lula heading into the second round of voting scheduled for October 25.

title: Houthi missile strike on al-Maashiq Palace kills two, ministers unhurt
content:
A Houthi missile strike on al‑Maashiq Palace, the Yemeni presidential palace, killed two people, Yemen’s information minister said. The attack involved ballistic missiles that hit the building.

The minister added that the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt in the strike.
summary: Houthi ballistic missiles hit al-Maashiq Palace, killing two people. Yemen's information minister said the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt.
author: BBC World

title: Whalefall review – slimy survival thriller traps us in a whale and struggles to make it digestible
content:
Austin Abrams stars in Whalefall, a 106-minute adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s acclaimed novel that follows a character trapped inside a sperm whale. The film, directed by Brian Duffield, is described as an overlong and flashback-heavy project that keeps audiences on edge only in moments. Abrams, noted as a Euphoria alum, appears in every scene of what is his second studio lead in a month, performing actions such as screaming and writhing within the confined space.

Critics note that while Abrams brings his considerable likability to the role, the script’s setup is too overstretched and silly to sustain interest for the full runtime. The review compares the premise to a single scene from Finding Nemo expanded into a feature film, suggesting the narrative fails to make the survival thriller digestible. Despite the grabby initial concept, the film struggles to generate genuine concern for the protagonist’s escape or the method he might use to achieve it.
summary: Austin Abrams gets eaten by a sperm whale in an overlong and flashback-heavy adaptation of Daniel Kraus’s hit novel that only has us on edge in momentsSpare a thought for poor Austin Abrams, who, having just endured the world’s worst, and gloopiest, courier assignment in Resident Evil, has now been trapped inside a sperm whale …The immensely likable Euphoria alum (has any show in recent memory provided quite as many genuine stars?) brings what he can to Brian Duffield’s rather soggy adaptation of Pulitzer prize-winner Daniel Kraus’s acclaimed novel Whalefall. But there’s not a great deal he can do, despite being in every scene of what’s his second studio lead in a month, other than scream and writhe and look understandably alarmed.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Sally Rooney’s stand on Palestine is brave and humane
content:
Sally Rooney, author of Normal People, has pledged to support Palestine Action, stating that royalties from her books and their BBC adaptations will be directed to the organization. The article argues that this commitment makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism laws, noting that it is rare for a published author to risk arrest in the UK for political beliefs or to face the possibility of having their books withdrawn from sale.

Rooney reportedly went into this situation with her eyes open, having made her intentions public in July. The text distinguishes her actions from other forms of political advocacy, such as writing essays, signing letters, or voicing support in interviews, which may carry social or professional costs but do not involve actively breaking terrorism laws. By choosing to financially support a proscribed organization, Rooney has selected a path that entails legal risks beyond those typically associated with public political expression.

The article highlights that while Rooney has suffered a tangible financial hit by pledging her royalties, the broader consequences of being effectively barred from and banned in the UK are innumerable. These include lost sales and opportunities that ripple out from her exclusion, representing a cost that is difficult to quantify compared to the fixed value of her royalty pledges.
summary: The Normal People author’s determination to support Palestine Action, even if it means that her books are withdrawn from sale in the UK, makes a mockery of Britain’s terrorism lawsIt’s hard to think of a published author in living memory who risked arrest in the UK for their political beliefs, hard to think of one whose books could be published anywhere but here. Sally Rooney went into this debacle with her eyes open: she said last July that royalties from her books, and their BBC adaptations, would be used to support Palestine Action.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Jesse Eisenberg’s 10 best film performances ranked as The Debut closes London film festival
content:
Jesse Eisenberg is set to close the London film festival with his new movie, The Debut, prompting a retrospective ranking of his ten best film performances. The article highlights Eisenberg’s recent work in Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of the Dostoevsky novella, where he delivers a split-personality performance.

In the film, Eisenberg portrays Simon, a shy and self-effacing computer programmer living in a grim future world who is ignored by his employers and co-worker Hannah, played by Mia Wasikowska. He also plays James, Simon’s confident and charismatic carbon copy who impresses his bosses and captivates Hannah. This dual role creates a dynamic where James’s success causes distress for Simon.
summary: The article ranks Jesse Eisenberg's top ten film roles as his new movie The Debut closes the London film festival. It highlights his split-personality performance in Richard Ayoade's adaptation of a Dostoevsky novella.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Paul McCartney concerned about appearing shorter than John Lennon in Beatles films
content:
Paul McCartney has expressed concern over a detail in Sam Mendes’ upcoming Beatles biopics, specifically regarding a fictional version of himself appearing marginally shorter than a fictional John Lennon. This comment emerged amid significant public discourse and fact-checking surrounding the four near-identical films, which have been scrutinized for creative choices and historical accuracy.

While other band members had previously remained largely quiet about the production, Ringo Starr previously discussed sitting down with Mendes to rework a scene, and McCartney had praised the guitar playing of actor Paul Mescal. McCartney’s recent remarks appear to mark a shift in the remaining Beatles’ silence, introducing what may be a new point of contention regarding the films’ portrayal of the band members.
summary: Paul McCartney has expressed concern about a fictional version of himself appearing shorter than John Lennon in Sam Mendes' Beatles biopics. This marks the first significant public complaint from a remaining Beatle regarding the production of the films.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Jimmy Kimmel jokes Trump may be bored by AI-generated social media videos
content: Jimmy Kimmel discussed President Donald Trump’s recent focus on AI-generated social media videos and cognitive tests. The host addressed these topics with only three weeks remaining until the US midterm elections. Kimmel made these comments while other hosts were on holiday.
summary: Jimmy Kimmel discussed President Donald Trump's focus on AI-generated social media videos and cognitive tests. He commented on Trump's online and offline antics with three weeks left before the US midterm elections.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Lance Oppenheim behind buzzy films Primetime and You Can See Everything
content:
Thirty-year-old Florida-born filmmaker Lance Oppenheim has produced two high-profile films poised to impact the upcoming awards season: the documentary You Can See Everything and the drama Primetime. The documentary, co-directed with Nathan Fielder, follows disgraced health-tech mogul Elizabeth Holmes for a month prior to her 11-year prison sentence for fraud and conspiracy. Described by Oppenheim as “head-spinning,” the three-hour film is shrouded in secrecy, with Variety magazine’s Oscar predictions listing one cast member only as “[Redacted].” It is expected to become the first documentary nominated for best picture.

Oppenheim’s other project, Primetime, stars Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen, the television figure known for ambushing individuals on the Dateline NBC segment To Catch a Predator. The article notes that Pattinson’s performance is generating significant Oscar buzz. The drama explores Hansen’s work between 2004 and 2007, a period when the segment was described as disreputable yet highly addictive, before Hansen launched various spin-offs. While some of these follow-up programs maintained a similar controversial appeal, others, such as a sting operation targeting bicycle thieves, did not.
summary: Thirty-year-old director Lance Oppenheim is making two major awards contenders, including a documentary about Elizabeth Holmes and a drama starring Robert Pattinson. The films challenge perceptions of reality and are expected to generate significant Oscar buzz.
author: Guardian Culture

title: PSG outclass Manchester City in Champions League as Aston Villa thrashes Fenerbahce
content:
Paris Saint-Germain asserted their status as the benchmark in European club football by defeating Manchester City during the Champions League’s return from the international break. The match marked a homecoming for Pep Guardiola’s team, but their performance was overshadowed by PSG’s display.

In other action, Prince William attended the match between his favorite team, Aston Villa, and Fenerbahce. The English club secured a decisive 6-0 victory in the contest.

The competition’s latest round also highlighted Italy’s search for a new saviour, while an Italian-German dilemma emerged as part of the broader narrative of the tournament.
summary: Paris Saint-Germain defeated Manchester City to demonstrate their status as the benchmark in European club football. Aston Villa secured a 6-0 victory over Fenerbahce in a match attended by Prince William.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Australia edges New Zealand in Rugby League World Cup opener
content:
Kalyn Ponga starred for New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup opener at Sydney’s Allianz Stadium, although Australia ultimately edged the match. The game served as a fiery demonstration that the tournament is up for grabs, highlighting the impact of new rules that encourage players to swap nations. This cultural shift has generated mixed reactions, delighting some while offending others, but the intense atmosphere on the pitch has been a win for both players and fans.

The opening ceremony featured an elaborate production with fireworks, lasers, and shimmering projections, transforming the stadium into a spectacle reminiscent of a Las Vegas casino. This event marked the beginning of a bold new era for the sport, which has significantly rejigged its tournament format. The number of competing nations was reduced from 16 to 10, and the total number of matches was boiled down from 31 to 18 to distill the talent pool.
summary: Australia defeated New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup opener at Allianz Stadium, where Kalyn Ponga starred for the Kiwis. The match marked the start of a reformed tournament that reduced competing nations from 16 to 10 and total matches from 31 to 18.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Alex Scott quits Disney+ role as Women’s Champions League presenter
content:
Former Football Focus host Alex Scott has departed from her position as a presenter for the Women’s Champions League coverage on Disney+. The departure was Scott’s decision, as she chooses to focus on other professional projects.

Among her new endeavors is the show One More Word WSL, which she will host alongside fellow former England internationals Anita Asante and Fara Williams. This move comes after Disney+ faced criticism following the opening round of the current season.
summary: Scott walking away to focus on other projectsDisney+ was criticised after opening round this seasonAlex Scott, the former Football Focus host, has left her role as a presenter of the Women’s Champions League coverage on Disney+. title: Tom Willis to face Gloucester as England No 8 depth debate intensifies
content:

Although England head coach Steve Borthwick has the option to select one player based outside England for the World Cup, the consensus suggests Jack Willis, the Toulouse captain, as the likely choice. However, the article notes that Borthwick would strongly prefer to select Tom Willis, whose departure for France following an enhanced contract was described as unprecedented.

Willis is currently performing at a high level for Bordeaux, with the source describing his impact as "pulling up trees, forests and anything else in his way." The piece emphasizes that England’s No 8 position lacks depth, making Willis a player Borthwick would value highly. The upcoming Champions Cup match serves to underscore the quality of rugby England is missing due to his absence from the domestic league.
summary: Tom Willis is set to play for Bordeaux against Gloucester in the Champions Cup, highlighting a significant gap in England's No 8 options. Steve Borthwick is reportedly considering selecting the Toulouse-based player for the World Cup despite his move to France.

content:

title: Trump cancels Hegseth's plan to livestream execution of Nidal Malik Hasan
content:
President Trump announced on Thursday that the planned livestreamed execution of Nidal Malik Hasan would not proceed. Hasan, a former U.S. Army major, was convicted of killing 13 people during the 2009 attack on Fort Hood.

content: Atlantic writer Josh Tyrangiel identifies Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos as the primary rivals in the race for control of outer space. Tyrangiel argues that the only genuine competition for these goals is between Musk and Bezos themselves.

content:

content: Reform leader Nigel Farage has defended his party's vetting process following the release of undercover footage showing party activists making racist comments. Farage stated that it is impossible to vet individuals for comments they may make in the future, responding to the revelations about the conduct of the party's local members.

content: Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) officials wrote to the Green Party regarding its motion that “Zionism is racism.” The motion was reported to the EHRC by Members of Parliament and antisemitism campaigners. The letter from the watchdog addresses the concerns raised by these parties over the motion’s content.

title: Aortic root enlargement technique lets surgeons implant valves at least two sizes larger
content: A small aortic root can restrict the size of the prosthetic valve implanted during aortic valve replacement. This limitation can result in a patient-prosthesis mismatch, where the new valve is too small for the patient’s body. Such a mismatch forces the heart to work against increased resistance, a condition associated with poorer clinical outcomes.
summary: A new aortic root enlargement technique enables surgeons to place prosthetic heart valves that are at least two sizes larger than previously possible. Using a larger valve helps avoid patient‑prosthesis mismatch, which is linked to poorer clinical outcomes when the valve is too small for the patient’s body.

title: GLP-1s Linked to Lower Psychiatric Risk in Schizophrenia and Type 2 Diabetes
content:
New research published in The Lancet Psychiatry indicates that treatment with glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) is associated with reduced risks of psychiatric hospitalization and emergency department visits among individuals diagnosed with both schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes.

The study found that these benefits were observed when comparing GLP-1 treatment to no GLP-1 treatment or the use of newer diabetes medications, suggesting a potential link between the conditions and a therapeutic avenue for managing associated risks.
summary: New research published in The Lancet Psychiatry found that GLP-1 treatment is associated with lower risks of psychiatric hospitalization and emergency visits in people with both schizophrenia and type 2 diabetes. This benefit was observed compared with no GLP-1 treatment or treatment with newer diabetes medications.

title: Study links children's caffeine intake to shorter sleep and brain development changes
content: A study led by researchers at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience (IoPPN) at King's College London has found that young people who consume more caffeine sleep less and exhibit minor differences in brain development. The research, published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, indicates that the majority of caffeine intake among these young participants came from soft drinks.
summary: A study led by King's College London researchers found that young people consuming more caffeine sleep less. The research also identified small differences in how their brains are developing.

title: California Health Survey Links 2025 Wildfires to Health Issues
content:
New annual data from the California Health Interview Survey (CHIS) released today offers a detailed examination of the health impacts of the 2025 wildfires on Californians. The survey also highlights concerning health trends affecting immigrants, low-income individuals, and transgender and gender-expansive communities.

The report identifies wildfires, heat waves, and barriers to accessing medical care as significant health-related challenges facing the state’s population. These findings provide a more precise understanding of how recent environmental events have influenced overall well-being in California.
summary: New annual California Health Interview Survey data released today examines the health impacts of the 2025 wildfires on Californians. The report also identifies troubling health trends among immigrants, low-income individuals, and transgender and gender-expansive communities.

title: Study Finds 1 in 4 Active-Duty US Army Men May Have Low Testosterone
content:
New research from the Pennington Biomedical Research Center, published this week in JAMA, indicates that approximately one in four active-duty male U.S. Army personnel may have a morning testosterone measurement below a commonly used clinical threshold. The study provides estimates of low testosterone screening results across the active-duty Army population.

These findings offer insight into the potential implications of implementing routine testosterone screening for military personnel.
summary: New research from Pennington Biomedical Research Center indicates that approximately one in four active-duty male U.S. Army personnel may have a morning testosterone measurement below a commonly used clinical threshold. The study, published in JAMA, provides estimates of low testosterone screening results to offer insight into the implications of routine screening for military personnel.

title: Intensive blood pressure control protects heart without added kidney failure risk
content: High blood pressure forces the heart to work harder to pump blood, a strain that can thicken the heart muscle and narrow arteries over time. This condition complicates cardiovascular health, and even in individuals with no other health conditions, a 20 mmHg rise in blood pressure doubles the risk of dying from heart disease.
summary: High blood pressure forces the heart to work harder, which can thicken the heart muscle and narrow arteries. A 20 mmHg rise in blood pressure doubles the risk of dying from heart disease even in people with no other health conditions.

title: Experts propose reframing traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries as chronic disorders
content:
A new paper published in The Lancet Neurology proposes a fundamental shift in the understanding and management of traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries in adults. Titled "Reframing traumatic brain injury and spinal cord injury as chronic multisystem disorders: toward integrated, long-term care," the article advocates for viewing these conditions as chronic multisystem disorders rather than acute events.

The proposal is authored by international experts from various institutions and disciplines. The paper aims to establish a framework for integrated, long-term care that aligns with the chronic nature of these injuries.
summary: A new paper in The Lancet Neurology proposes a fundamental shift in how traumatic brain and spinal cord injuries in adults are understood and managed. International experts suggest reframing these conditions as chronic multisystem disorders to enable integrated, long-term care.

content:

content: NHS England has issued new guidance stating that trans patients should receive care on single-sex hospital wards or bays that correspond to their biological sex. The directive specifies that hospital spaces should be allocated based on biological sex rather than gender identity.
summary: New NHS England guidance states that trans patients should be cared for on single-sex hospital wards or bays. The spaces must align with the patient's biological sex.

content:

title: X-rays and machine learning reveal palm-leaf manuscript preparation traces
content: Palm-leaf manuscripts used across South and Southeast Asia for centuries to record religious, literary, legal, and scientific texts have revealed traces of their preparation techniques through X-ray imaging and machine learning. Prior to inscription, these leaves underwent extensive preparation, with processing methods differing by region and potentially creating distinct material signatures.
summary: Researchers used X-rays and machine learning to detect material signatures from the preparation of palm-leaf manuscripts. These processing techniques varied by region and were required before inscribing religious, literary, legal, and scientific texts in South and Southeast Asia.

title: Laser pulses bring order to tiny electrically charged islands in quantum crystal
content:
Physicists at Auburn University have used laser light flashes to organize tiny electrically charged "islands" within a crystal. This discovery addresses a decades-old question regarding how the material organizes itself.

The findings also demonstrate how light can be used to control the material's behavior, representing a step toward exploring new technologies for processing and storing information.
summary: Physicists at Auburn University used flashes of laser light to bring order to tiny electrically charged islands inside a crystal. The discovery answers a decades-old question about how the material organizes itself and shows that light could control its behavior, a step toward new technologies for processing and storing information.

title: Survey asks teachers what occupation teaching resembles, answers from three countries
content:
A recent open‑ended question asked teachers, “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?” and gathered responses from three different countries.  

The inquiry yielded three distinct answers, each reflecting the perspective of respondents in the respective nation.  

The varied replies illustrate how perceptions of the teaching profession can differ depending on where educators live.
summary: The piece reports three answers from three countries to the open‑ended question “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?”. The responses show how perceptions of teaching vary by location.
author: Phys.org

title: India's cobras share genetic ties across the mainland, while Sri Lankan cobras form a distinct genetic lineage
content:
The spectacled cobra (Naja naja), one of India’s "big four" snakes responsible for most serious snakebite cases, is currently classified as a single species inhabiting much of South Asia. While regional populations exhibit differences in color, hood markings, and venom, the evolutionary relationships among these groups have remained unclear.

A new study published in Molecular Phylogenetics and Evolution clarifies that cobras on the Indian mainland share genetic ties, whereas Sri Lankan cobras constitute a distinct genetic lineage. The research helps identify which regional populations represent separate evolutionary groups and provides insights into when and where they diverged from their ancestors.
summary: The spectacled cobra (Naja naja) is one of India's "big four" snakes responsible for most serious snakebite cases. It is currently considered one species, which lives across much of South Asia, with regional differences in color, hood markings and venom.
author: Phys.org

title: Probiotic with breast milk sugars cuts respiratory infection risk in formula-fed babies
content:
Formula-fed infants generally face a higher susceptibility to infections compared to their breast-fed peers. However, research indicates that adding a specific probiotic supplement to their diet can significantly reduce the likelihood of these babies contracting respiratory viruses.

The probiotic supplement utilized in this context contains sugars derived from breast milk. This addition effectively lowered the risk of respiratory infections among the formula-fed infants who received it.
summary: Formula-fed babies face a higher risk of infections, but a specific probiotic supplement reduces this vulnerability. The supplement contains sugars from breast milk and was shown to slash the risk of respiratory viruses in these infants.

title: Study examines impact of government-private digital partnerships on public trust
content:
A new study investigates the impact of digital platforms on public trust in government, focusing on the collaborative efforts between state entities and private companies. These partnerships are designed to deliver public services through online channels, creating a shared digital infrastructure for citizen engagement.

The research specifically examines how the involvement of the private sector in the provision of these digital services influences the level of trust that individuals place in their respective governments.
summary: Governments and private companies frequently collaborate to deliver public services online. A new study investigates how these partnerships influence people's trust in government.

title: Strokes nearly double among adults 20-54, driven by blocked vessels
content:
Stroke rates among adults aged 20 to 54 have nearly doubled over the past three decades. Recent research indicates that blocked blood vessels in the brain are a primary driver of this increase. Additionally, younger stroke patients are increasingly presenting with high blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use.

Although survival rates for these patients have improved, the rising incidence means more young adults may face the long-term consequences of stroke.
summary: Stroke rates among adults aged 20 to 54 have nearly doubled over nearly three decades, with blocked blood vessels accounting for much of the increase. High blood pressure, diabetes, and substance use also became more common among younger stroke patients, though improved survival rates mean more may face lasting consequences.

title: Scientists engineer plant immune receptor to fight crop-threatening fungus
content:
Scientists have identified a potential new defense against a destructive fungus that endangers global rice, wheat, and barley production. The research team engineered a specialized plant immune receptor designed to recognize multiple fungal threats simultaneously, offering a novel approach to crop protection.

This breakthrough aims to develop crops with robust and durable disease resistance. Such advancements could help safeguard the global food supply, which faces growing risks from expanding fungal infections and the impacts of climate change.
summary: Researchers developed a new plant immune receptor that can recognize multiple fungal threats simultaneously. This breakthrough aims to create crops with long-lasting disease resistance to protect the global food supply.

title: Late-night eating linked to up to 30% higher liver disease risk
content:
A study led by Oregon Health & Science University suggests that eating late at night may increase the risk of liver disease. Researchers analyzed data from nearly 200,000 individuals to examine the relationship between meal timing and liver health.

The findings indicate that participants who regularly ate after dinner or around bedtime had a 20% to 30% higher risk of developing liver conditions. These conditions included fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.
summary: A study led by Oregon Health & Science University analyzed data from nearly 200,000 people to examine dietary habits. The researchers found that regularly eating after dinner or around bedtime is associated with a 20% to 30% higher risk of liver disease, including fatty liver disease and cirrhosis.

title: Baylor study finds brain processes language under general anesthesia
content:
Baylor researchers have discovered that the human brain retains significant cognitive capabilities even under general anesthesia. The study reveals that unconscious individuals can still analyze language, distinguish between different word types, and predict the progression of a story.

These findings challenge existing scientific understanding of consciousness by demonstrating that the unconscious brain is far more functional than previously realized.
summary: Baylor researchers discovered that the human brain can analyze language and predict story elements while under general anesthesia. These findings challenge current understanding of consciousness by showing the unconscious brain is more capable than previously realized.

title: Arctic sea ice hits new low as scientists warn of ice-free summer before 2050
content: Satellite records indicate that Arctic sea ice is declining in both winter and summer, with the remaining ice becoming thinner, younger, and more susceptible to melting. Although recent data shows a slowdown in summer ice losses, scientists warn that the Arctic region could reach a nearly ice-free state during the summer season before 2050.
summary: Satellite records show Arctic sea ice is shrinking in both winter and summer, becoming thinner and younger. Scientists warn the region could experience a nearly ice-free summer before 2050 despite a recent slowdown in summer losses.

title: How an accelerating Earth led experts to adopt the leap hour
content:
Delegates from 69 countries voted on Thursday at a conference in France to replace the leap second with a leap hour. The decision was made by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures, which maintains global standards for time, weight, and distance. Experts concluded that the existing leap second system is no longer tenable after decades of discussion regarding its impact on computer systems.

While the leap hour has been adopted as the new standard, the first occurrence is not expected for thousands of years.
summary: International delegates agree leap second no longer tenable, but first leap hour not likely to happen for thousands of yearsAfter decades of discussion, quibbling and worrying about clocks in computer systems, the world’s official timekeepers have voted to replace what many viewed as a tiresome correction: the leap second. It’s time, they say, for the leap hour.

title: Chandra Finds Possible Origin of Treble Clef Waves
content:
NASA’s Chandra X-Ray Observatory captured an image on October 14, 2026, revealing a formation of radio waves that resembles a treble clef. Researchers utilized data from the Chandra observatory to investigate the origins of this distinctive cosmic structure.

The study suggests that the Treble Clef formation is likely the result of an outburst from a supermassive black hole followed by a collision between two galaxy clusters.
summary: NASA's Chandra X-Ray Observatory captured an image of a radio wave formation resembling a treble clef. Researchers determined this structure likely resulted from a supermassive black hole outburst followed by a collision of two galaxy clusters.

title: NASA Confirms Artemis II Heat Shield Performed as Expected After Lunar Mission
content:

Following the mission, additional engineering data analysis of the Orion spacecraft’s heat shield confirmed that the component performed as expected, aligning with initial data findings.

The analysis specifically focused on measuring the thermal protection capabilities of the heat shield to verify its rigorous performance during reentry.
summary: NASA's Artemis II mission successfully sent four astronauts around the Moon and returned them safely to Earth. Additional engineering data analysis confirmed that the Orion spacecraft's heat shield performed as expected during the mission.

content:

The awards are part of NASA’s Minority University Research and Education Project (MUREP) Space Technology Artemis Research (M-STAR) initiative. Under this program, each selected institution will receive up to $1 million.
summary: NASA selected 12 U.S. institutions to receive a total of $12 million under the Minority University Research and Education Project Space Technology Artemis Research (M‑STAR) initiative. content:

summary: Registration is open for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, a two-day global event scheduled for November 14 and 15. Teams will work to create solutions inspired by NASA exploration goals using the agency's free and open data.

title: NASA to conduct low‑altitude flights over Texas farmland to measure emissions
content:
NASA will conduct low‑altitude research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will carry out the missions, measuring gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations.

The flights aim to quantify agricultural emissions, which represent an important and understudied part of Earth’s land and atmosphere systems. The FarmFlux mission will deploy the aircraft for this purpose.
summary: A NASA Dynamic Aviation A200 aircraft will conduct low‑flying research flights over farmland near Transit, Texas, from Thursday, Oct. 22, through Monday, Nov. 9. The flights will measure gaseous and particulate emissions from animal feeding operations as part of the FarmFlux mission.

title: Nvidia Announces RTX Spark Laptops to Run All Windows Apps on Arm
content:
Nvidia is set to launch its first wave of RTX Spark laptops on Friday, October 16, after a 14‑year gap since the company’s last attempt to power a Windows PC. The original Microsoft Surface, which ran a stripped‑down version of Windows on an Nvidia Tegra chip, failed to gain traction and forced Microsoft to write off $900 million in inventory because the Arm‑based chip could not run existing Windows applications.

This new generation of RTX Spark laptops is positioned to address that shortcoming. Nvidia claims the chip will run “everything,” including major software suites such as Adobe and Office, on Arm‑powered Windows PCs.

content:

The new Kaleido 4 technology addresses some of Kaleido 3’s shortcomings by delivering improved color reproduction, better contrast, and faster screen refreshes.

content:
